author: Sharon Sanders
title: Out of the past: March 12
text:
HistoryMarch 12, 2026
Out of the past: March 12
From river fishing pacts and a new Cape Girardeau bookstore to jail-site debates, anti-spanking pleas, armed boys and Billy Sunday’s denunciation of card games, March 12 memories resurface.
2001
The Mississippi River has become more user friendly for anglers, following an agreement between the Illinois Department of Natural Resources and the Missouri Department of Conservation; the pact, which took effect March 1, allows anglers from either state to fish anywhere within the 331 miles of Illinois-Missouri boundary waters of the Mississippi or its backwaters.
Roger and Linda Hagan of Altenburg have opened Hagan’s Store, a book shop at 437 Broadway in Cape Girardeau, offering new and used, hardback and paperback books.
1976
A six-acre tract of industrial land in north Jackson is no longer available to Cape Girardeau County as a site for a new county jail; County Court Presiding Judge Ervin Hobbs told the other members of court yesterday he had asked Mayor Carlton Meyer whether the site was available after Associate Judge J. Ronald Fischer suggested that the property, owned by the Jackson Industrial Development Committee, again be considered as location for the facility; the unavailability of the site means the court will likely proceed with construction of the jail on the city-owned property across the street from the present jail.
Dr. John E. Valuseks, a psychologist addressing a session of the Southeast Missouri District Teachers Association yesterday, declared spanking is the major “seed bed” for much of the world’s violence; he called for the abolishment of corporal punishment in schools and homes.
1951
Two boys, 13 and 14, who “hate the cops”, were taken into custody by police yesterday morning, and they were found to be armed with. .22 rifle, which they said they were going to use to shoot any officer who came after them; the pair, described by police as harsh-speaking youngsters, were found in a barn on Marietta Street, west of Perryville Road, where they had been living for a week; besides the rifle, the boys were stocked with canned goods, blankets, a camera and numerous other articles; one of the youths is a ward of the juvenile court at Fredericktown, while the other lives here with his grandparents.
The Cape County Selective Service Board, which dispatches its March contingent of 23 men to St. Louis for induction into the Army, will move Thursday to new quarters on the first floor of the Harris Building, 234 Broadway; since the draft was revived in 1948 after a short post-war lapse, the office has been on the second floor of the Buckner-Ragsdale building; in World War II, it was at Jackson.
1926
Speaking to a crowd of 3,500 last night at the tabernacle, evangelist Billy Sunday took special aim at card playing; Sunday denounced “society card games for prizes,” saying, “Why whist-bridge is only a new name for poker. You sit around and play for prizes and there isn’t a bit of difference from playing for money in a gambling house. You call a gambler a crook. So are you. He plays for $5 and more stakes; you play for prizes. What’s the difference?”
A total of 4,654 Cape Girardeans have registered to vote at the approaching municipal elections; the city’s first registration of eligible voters came to an end last night; the total exceeds by 2,140 the number of votes cast in the last city election in 1924.
Southeast Missourian librarian Sharon Sanders compiles the information for the daily Out of the Past column. She also writes a weekend column called “From the Morgue” that showcases interesting historical stories from the newspaper.
